Findings: Minor: WordCounter.cs has an explicit `using System;` even though ImplicitUsings is enabled in the csproj — harmless but redundant given the project settings.

Char-by-char iteration via char.IsLetterOrDigit(char) will not correctly classify astral-plane (surrogate-pair) letters/digits as single code points, but this is explicitly flagged as an open question in the spec and the Summary explicitly says 'per char.IsLetterOrDigit semantics', so the chosen approach is a reasonable, spec-consistent interpretation rather than a defect.
Strengths: CountWords implementation is a tight, linear single-pass state machine (inWord flag) with no unnecessary complexity — appropriately small and YAGNI-compliant for the stated requirements.
Null check throws ArgumentNullException as required; empty/whitespace/punctuation-only inputs correctly return 0 via the same simple loop logic without special-casing.
Namespace/class nesting (namespace WordCounter { class WordCounter }) matches the required fully-qualified WordCounter.WordCounter exactly.
XML doc comments on the class and method are concise and accurately describe behavior and the thrown exception.

Visible tests directly mirror every acceptance criterion (null throw, empty, whitespace, punctuation-only, mixed alnum runs, accented letters, tabs/newlines, cross-assembly public accessibility check), giving strong confidence the implementation satisfies the spec.
csproj correctly targets net10.0 with Nullable and ImplicitUsings enabled, matching the 'the solution must be a .NET 10 class library' requirement.
Summary: The implementation is a small, correct, and idiomatic realization of the spec: a single-pass char.IsLetterOrDigit state machine that satisfies every requirement and acceptance criterion, with matching namespace/class naming and solid test coverage. No maintainability, correctness, or design issues beyond a trivial redundant using directive.
